lessons.title: Your body's wiring
lessons.fact: The nervous system is your body's fast messaging network. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system (CNS), the boss. Nerves branching out to the rest of the body form the peripheral nervous system (PNS). It senses what is happening, decides what to do, and tells muscles and glands to act.
lessons.rick: Brain and spinal cord are HQ, nerves are the cables. Yours is mostly *burp* buffering, but the hardware's standard.

lessons.title: Meet the neuron
lessons.fact: Neurons are nerve cells. Dendrites are branches that receive signals. The cell body (soma) holds the nucleus. One long axon carries the electrical signal away from the cell body to the axon terminals. There the signal crosses a synapse to the next cell using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.
lessons.rick: Dendrites listen, axon talks. Like me at parties, except the axon has something worth saying.

lessons.title: The big brain parts
lessons.fact: The cerebrum is the largest part, split into left and right hemispheres, each with 4 main lobes: frontal (planning, movement, personality), parietal (touch), temporal (hearing, memory) and occipital (vision). The cerebellum at the back handles balance and coordination. The brainstem regulates breathing and heart rate.
lessons.rick: Frontal lobe: decisions. Yours clearly called in sick. Cerebellum: balance. Mine's pickled, hence the wobble.

lessons.title: Spinal cord and reflexes
lessons.fact: The spinal cord runs inside the backbone and carries messages between brain and body. Sensory nerves bring information in; motor nerves send commands out to muscles. Touch a hot stove and a spinal reflex pulls your hand back before your brain even feels the pain. The skull and vertebrae protect it all.
lessons.rick: Reflexes skip the brain entirely. Explains how you've survived this long, genius.

questions.q: Which two organs make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
questions.explain: The CNS is the brain plus the spinal cord. The nerves that branch out to the rest of the body form the peripheral nervous system (PNS), not the CNS.
questions.rick: Brain plus spinal cord. Two parts. TWO. Even a Meeseeks could hold that in memory before poofing.

questions.q: What is the main signaling cell of the nervous system called?
questions.explain: Neurons carry electrical and chemical signals. A nephron is the kidney's filtering unit, an erythrocyte is a red blood cell and an osteocyte is a bone cell.
questions.rick: Neuron. Nephron is kidney. Two letters apart, a whole *burp* universe of difference, Morty-brain.

questions.q: Which part of a neuron carries the signal AWAY from the cell body?
questions.explain: The axon conducts the signal away from the cell body toward the axon terminals. Dendrites do the opposite: they bring incoming signals toward the cell body.
questions.rick: Axon: away. Both start with A. I'm literally spoon-feeding you mnemonics here.

questions.q: Which part of the brain mainly coordinates balance and smooth movement?
questions.explain: The cerebellum, tucked at the back under the cerebrum, coordinates balance, posture and smooth movement. The occipital lobe handles vision and the temporal lobe hearing and memory.
questions.rick: Cerebellum. Why do drunks wobble? Booze messes with it. I'm conducting ongoing field research.

questions.q: Which lobe of the brain mainly processes vision?
questions.explain: The primary visual cortex sits in the occipital lobe at the back of the head. Your eyes are at the front, but the signals travel all the way to the back.
questions.rick: Eyes in front, vision in the back. Your body's wiring is almost as dumb as your questions. Occipital.

questions.q: Neurons pass signals across a synapse using chemicals called:
questions.explain: Neurotransmitters (like acetylcholine or dopamine) are released into the tiny synaptic gap and act on the next cell within milliseconds. Hormones are chemical messengers too, but they travel in the blood.
questions.rick: Neurotransmitters. Hormones go by blood, the slow mail. Synapses use the express portal.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls automatic functions like breathing and heart rate?
questions.explain: The brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla) connects the brain to the spinal cord and runs vital automatic functions such as breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.
questions.rick: Brainstem. Keeps you breathing without your help. Thank god, because your help is *burp* useless.

questions.q: You touch a hot stove and pull your hand away before you feel pain. Why?
choices: The skin contracts the arm muscles directly, without nerves
A spinal cord reflex acts before the brain registers pain
The occipital lobe sees the heat and reacts first
The arm muscles sense the heat and decide to move
questions.explain: In a reflex arc the sensory nerve signals the spinal cord, which directly activates motor neurons to the muscle. The message to the brain, where pain is actually felt, arrives a moment later.

questions.q: Click the dendrites, the branches that receive incoming signals.
questions.explain: Dendrites are the branching extensions around the cell body. They collect signals from other neurons and pass them toward the cell body.
questions.rick: Dendrites: the antennae. Like Wi-Fi, except it actually picks up a signal. Unlike you.

questions.q: Click the cerebellum.
questions.explain: The cerebellum ('little brain') sits at the back, below the occipital lobe and behind the brainstem. It coordinates balance and smooth movement.

questions.q: Click the frontal lobe.
questions.explain: The frontal lobe is the front part of each cerebral hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus. It handles planning, decisions, personality and voluntary movement.

lessons.title: Divisions of the system
lessons.fact: The PNS has 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle. The autonomic system runs smooth muscle, heart muscle and glands: sympathetic = fight or flight (faster heart, dilated pupils), parasympathetic = rest and digest (slower heart, digestion).
lessons.rick: Sympathetic: flee the Galactic Federation. Parasympathetic: digest your Szechuan sauce afterwards.

lessons.title: The action potential
lessons.fact: At rest the inside of a neuron is about -70 mV, kept by K+ leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP). At threshold (about -55 mV) voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ rushes in and the inside goes positive (about +30 mV). Then K+ flows out to repolarize. It's all-or-none.
lessons.rick: All-or-none, like my commitment to science. Hit threshold or *burp* go home.

lessons.title: Myelin and the synapse
lessons.fact: Myelin insulates axons: Schwann cells make it in the PNS, oligodendrocytes in the CNS. The impulse jumps between gaps called nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), which is much faster. At the axon terminal the impulse opens Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ entry makes vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synapse.
lessons.rick: Saltatory conduction: the signal portal-hops node to node. I invented that. Probably. In some universe.

lessons.title: Brain regions, upgraded
lessons.fact: The brainstem has 3 parts: midbrain, pons and medulla. The medulla, lowest and continuous with the spinal cord, holds centers for heart rate, blood pressure and breathing. Cortex is outer gray matter (cell bodies); white matter is myelinated axons. Each cerebral hemisphere mainly controls the OPPOSITE side of the body.
lessons.rick: Left brain runs the right hand. Crossed wiring. Like your priorities, except it works.

questions.q: What is the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron?
questions.explain: At rest the inside of a neuron is about -70 mV relative to the outside. +30 mV is roughly the peak of an action potential, when the inside briefly turns positive.
questions.rick: Minus seventy. Negative, like my outlook on your career. +30 is the spike peak, genius.

questions.q: During the rising (depolarization) phase of an action potential, which ion rushes INTO the neuron?
questions.explain: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ flows in down its concentration and electrical gradients, making the inside positive. K+ flowing OUT is what repolarizes the cell afterwards.
questions.rick: Sodium in, potassium out. Salt goes into the cell like it goes on my margarita glass.

questions.q: Compared with a stimulus just above threshold, a sustained stimulus well above threshold makes a neuron fire action potentials that are:
choices: Graded in size, like a dimmer switch
The same size, but more frequent
Slower to travel down the axon
questions.explain: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold (about -55 mV) is reached, every spike has the same size and shape. A stronger stimulus is coded by MORE spikes per second (frequency coding), not bigger ones. Graded potentials are the ones that vary in size.
questions.rick: All-or-none, genius. Neurons don't shout louder, they just repeat themselves faster. Like me, *burp* on a bender.

questions.q: Which cells make myelin in the central nervous system?
questions.explain: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons, and one can wrap segments of many axons. Schwann cells are the PNS version, each myelinating one segment of one axon. Astrocytes support neurons; microglia are immune cells.
questions.rick: Oligodendrocytes in the CNS, Schwann cells outside. Mix them up and I portal you somewhere with no textbooks.

questions.q: What is saltatory conduction?
choices: The impulse jumping from one node of Ranvier to the next
The impulse traveling backward to the dendrites
Salt being pumped into the axon terminal
questions.explain: In myelinated axons the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, so it effectively jumps from node to node. That makes conduction much faster than in unmyelinated axons.
questions.rick: Saltare is Latin for 'to jump'. Nothing to do with salt. Put down the pretzels, Morty-brain.

questions.q: Which effect is caused by the sympathetic (fight or flight) system?
choices: Slower heart rate and constricted pupils
Contraction of the bladder to empty it
Faster heart rate and dilated pupils
questions.explain: Sympathetic activity raises heart rate, dilates pupils and airways, and shifts blood to muscles. Slowing the heart, constricting pupils, digestion and bladder emptying are parasympathetic (rest and digest) effects.
questions.rick: Fight or flight: heart pounding, pupils huge. Basically my face every time Unity calls.

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves does a human have?
questions.explain: There are 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. 12 is the number of cranial nerve pairs; 33 is roughly the number of vertebrae.
questions.rick: Thirty-one. Twelve is the cranial nerves. Write it down, your memory's a *burp* sieve.

questions.q: What directly triggers release of neurotransmitter from the axon terminal?
choices: Na+ being pumped out of the terminal
Cl- flowing out of the terminal
questions.explain: The arriving action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. Ca2+ entry triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and dump neurotransmitter into the cleft.
questions.rick: Calcium is the trigger. No calcium, no release. Like me without booze: zero output.

questions.q: Click the myelin sheath.
questions.explain: Myelin is the fatty insulating wrap around the axon, made by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS). It speeds conduction by letting the impulse jump between nodes.
questions.rick: The fatty insulation on the cable. Lose it and signals crawl. Like your reading speed.

questions.q: Click the lobe that contains the primary visual cortex.
questions.explain: The occipital lobe at the back of the cerebrum receives visual input relayed from the eyes through the thalamus. Damage here can blind part of the visual field even with healthy eyes.
questions.rick: Vision lives in the back of your head. Eyes in front, screen in back. Nature's a lousy engineer.

questions.q: Click the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.
questions.explain: The medulla oblongata sits below the pons and merges into the spinal cord. It holds vital centers for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, so damage here is often fatal.
questions.rick: Medulla. Break it and the lights go out. Permanently. Don't, uh, test that.

lessons.title: Channels and refractory periods
lessons.fact: At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+, so the resting potential sits near K+'s equilibrium potential (about -90 mV). Spikes start at the axon hillock/initial segment, rich in Na+ channels. Na+ channel inactivation causes the absolute refractory period; lingering K+ efflux causes the relative one.
lessons.rick: Na+ channels need a nap after firing. Absolute refractory period. You have one too: it's called your life.

lessons.title: Upper vs lower motor neurons
lessons.fact: Upper motor neurons (UMN) in motor cortex (notably the precentral gyrus) form the corticospinal tract; most cross at the pyramidal decussation (lower medulla) to reach anterior horn lower motor neurons (LMN). UMN lesion: spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign. LMN lesion: flaccid weakness, atrophy, fasciculations.
lessons.rick: Upper motor neuron down: stiff and jumpy. Lower: floppy and twitchy. Like me before and after *burp* coffee.

lessons.title: Sensory pathways
lessons.fact: The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex, mapped as a homunculus with huge face and hands. Fine touch, vibration and proprioception ascend the dorsal columns on the same side and cross in the medulla. Pain and temperature fibers cross within 1-2 segments and ascend in the spinothalamic tract.
lessons.rick: Dorsal columns cross high, pain crosses low. Two tracts, two rules. Your brain has room for two, right?

lessons.title: Transmitters and receptors
lessons.fact: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory transmitter; GABA the main inhibitory one (glycine in the spinal cord). Acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, and on muscarinic receptors at parasympathetic targets. Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine.
lessons.rick: Glutamate floors the gas, GABA hits the brakes. Your brain's mostly brakes, apparently.

questions.q: The absolute refractory period of an action potential is mainly due to:
choices: Voltage-gated K+ channels still being open
questions.explain: After opening, Na+ channels enter an inactivated state and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, so no new spike is possible. Still-open K+ channels (hyperpolarization) explain the RELATIVE refractory period.
questions.rick: Inactivated Na+ channels. K+ is the relative period. Absolute versus relative, like my genius versus yours.

questions.q: Why is the neuronal resting membrane potential close to the K+ equilibrium potential?
choices: The Na+/K+ pump directly generates most of the voltage
At rest the membrane is far more permeable to Na+ than to K+
K+ is actively pumped out of the cell, leaving it negative
At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to other ions
questions.explain: K+ leak channels make the resting membrane most permeable to K+, pulling the potential toward E(K+), about -90 mV; a small Na+ leak pulls it up to about -70 mV. The pump's direct electrogenic share is only a few mV.
questions.rick: Permeability rules, genius. The pump just maintains gradients. It's the janitor, not the CEO.

questions.q: Right-sided spastic weakness, hyperreflexia and an upgoing plantar reflex (Babinski sign). Where is the lesion most likely?
questions.explain: Spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski are upper motor neuron signs. Corticospinal fibers in the left internal capsule have not crossed yet, so a lesion there hits the right body. Anterior horn and nerve lesions give LMN signs.
questions.rick: UMN signs, opposite side, above the crossing. Left capsule, right body. Wiring 101, dummy.

questions.q: Where do most corticospinal tract fibers cross to the opposite side?
choices: Pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla
Anterior white commissure at each spinal level

questions.q: Pain and temperature from the LEFT foot ascend the spinal cord mainly in which tract and on which side?
questions.explain: Pain and temperature fibers synapse in the dorsal horn, and the second-order axons cross within about 1-2 segments to ascend in the contralateral spinothalamic tract. Dorsal columns carry touch and vibration on the same side.
questions.rick: Pain crosses early. Left foot, right cord. Like you, it switches sides at the first sign of *burp* trouble.

questions.q: Autoimmune destruction of CNS myelin (made by oligodendrocytes) is the hallmark of which disease?
questions.explain: Multiple sclerosis is immune-mediated demyelination of the CNS. Guillain-Barre targets PERIPHERAL myelin (Schwann cells), ALS kills motor neurons, and myasthenia gravis attacks ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.rick: MS: CNS myelin. Guillain-Barre: PNS myelin. Same crime, different jurisdiction.

questions.q: Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release which neurotransmitter onto their targets?
questions.explain: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers mostly release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors (exception: sweat glands get ACh). The adrenal medulla, not the neurons, secretes mostly epinephrine into the blood.
questions.rick: Norepinephrine. Epinephrine is the adrenal medulla's job. Different employees, genius.

questions.q: What is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain?
questions.explain: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain; glycine plays that role mainly in the spinal cord and brainstem. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter.

questions.q: Click the cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the cell body.
questions.explain: The axon hillock leads into the initial segment, which is packed with voltage-gated Na+ channels, so this hillock/initial-segment trigger zone is where summed inputs usually reach threshold and the spike starts.
questions.rick: The trigger zone. Every input gets summed here, then it fires or doesn't. Decisive. Unlike you.

questions.q: Click a gap in the myelin where the action potential is regenerated.
questions.explain: Nodes of Ranvier are short unmyelinated gaps packed with voltage-gated Na+ channels. The spike regenerates at each node and jumps to the next (saltatory conduction).

questions.q: Click the primary motor cortex.
questions.explain: The primary motor cortex is the precentral gyrus, the ridge just in front of the central sulcus in the frontal lobe. Its upper motor neurons drive voluntary movement of the opposite side of the body.

questions.q: Click the primary somatosensory cortex.
questions.explain: The primary somatosensory cortex is the postcentral gyrus, just behind the central sulcus in the parietal lobe. It maps touch, pain, temperature and position from the opposite side of the body.

lessons.title: Stroke syndromes
lessons.fact: MCA stroke: contralateral face and arm weakness and numbness (more than leg), plus aphasia if the dominant (usually left) side, neglect if nondominant. ACA: contralateral leg more than arm. PCA: contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Basilar artery occlusion infarcting the ventral pons: locked-in syndrome.
lessons.rick: Know the artery, know the deficit. The brain's a map, and strokes are me spilling *burp* whiskey on it.

lessons.title: Aphasias
lessons.fact: Broca aphasia (dominant inferior frontal gyrus): non-fluent, effortful speech, comprehension largely intact. Wernicke aphasia (posterior superior temporal gyrus): fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension, often unaware. Conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus): fluent, comprehends, but can't repeat.

lessons.title: Spinal cord lesions
lessons.fact: Brown-Sequard (hemisection), below the lesion: same-side spastic weakness and loss of vibration/position sense, opposite-side loss of pain and temperature. Syringomyelia: bilateral cape-like pain/temperature loss. B12 deficiency: dorsal columns plus lateral corticospinal tracts. ALS: UMN and LMN signs, no sensory loss.
lessons.rick: Hemisect a cord and the symptoms split sides. Like a breakup: each side keeps different stuff.

lessons.title: Toxins at the synapse
lessons.fact: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks ACh release: descending flaccid paralysis. Tetanus toxin blocks GABA and glycine release from spinal inhibitory interneurons: spastic paralysis, lockjaw. Lambert-Eaton: antibodies to presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Myasthenia gravis: antibodies to postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors.

questions.q: Sudden right face and arm weakness; she speaks in short, effortful phrases but follows commands. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.explain: Face and arm more than leg points to MCA territory on the lateral cortex; non-fluent speech with intact comprehension is Broca aphasia, so it's the dominant (left) hemisphere. ACA would hit the leg; PCA causes visual field loss.
questions.rick: Face, arm, Broca: left MCA. The most common stroke on the exam, and you still hesitated?

questions.q: Sudden weakness and numbness of the right leg, with the face and arm largely spared. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.explain: The leg and foot areas of motor and sensory cortex lie on the medial surface of the hemisphere, supplied by the ACA. Right leg means left hemisphere. MCA strokes hit face and arm more than leg.
questions.rick: Leg area's on the medial surface, ACA turf. Left artery, right leg. Crossed wires, as always, genius.

questions.q: A patient speaks fluently and understands well but cannot repeat a phrase. Damage to which structure is most likely?
questions.explain: Conduction aphasia: the arcuate fasciculus linking Wernicke and Broca areas is damaged, so repetition fails while fluency and comprehension are relatively spared. Broca gives non-fluent speech; Wernicke gives poor comprehension.

questions.q: A stab wound hemisects the LEFT half of the spinal cord at T10. Which deficit is expected below the lesion?
choices: Loss of pain and temperature on the right
Loss of vibration sense on the right
Loss of pain and temperature on the left

questions.q: An infant fed honey develops constipation, poor feeding and descending flaccid paralysis. What is the toxin's mechanism?
choices: Cleaving SNARE proteins to block ACh release
Blocking GABA and glycine release from interneurons
Blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels in axons

questions.q: A farmer with a dirty puncture wound and no tetanus shots develops lockjaw and painful spasms. The toxin blocks transmitter release mainly from:
choices: Alpha motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction
Inhibitory spinal interneurons, such as Renshaw cells

questions.q: A strict vegan has macrocytic anemia, lost vibration and position sense in the legs, and spastic weakness. Which cord regions are damaged?

questions.explain: Broca area is in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, just above the lateral sulcus. Damage causes expressive (Broca) aphasia: halting speech, intact comprehension, impaired repetition.

questions.explain: The central sulcus divides the frontal from the parietal lobe; the precentral (motor) gyrus lies in front of it and the postcentral (sensory) gyrus behind. The lateral sulcus instead separates off the temporal lobe.

lessons.title: Chemical messengers
lessons.fact: Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and released into the blood. They travel everywhere, but only cells with the matching receptor respond. Hormones act more slowly than nerve signals, but their effects usually last longer. Main glands: pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, ovaries or testes.

lessons.title: The master gland
lessons.fact: The pituitary is a pea-sized gland hanging below the brain. It is called the master gland because its hormones control other glands, like the thyroid and adrenals. It also makes growth hormone, which drives growth in childhood. The pituitary itself takes orders from the hypothalamus, a brain area just above it.

lessons.title: Thyroid and adrenals
lessons.fact: The butterfly-shaped thyroid in the front of the neck makes thyroid hormone, which sets your metabolic rate (how fast cells burn energy); it needs iodine. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. They make adrenaline (epinephrine) for fight or flight, and cortisol, a stress hormone.

lessons.title: Sugar and sex hormones
lessons.fact: The pancreas makes insulin, which lowers blood sugar by helping cells take in glucose, and glucagon, which raises it. Diabetes mellitus means high blood sugar: type 1 = little or no insulin made; type 2 = cells respond poorly to insulin and the pancreas can't keep up. Testes make testosterone; ovaries, estrogen and progesterone.

choices: Through the air in the lungs

questions.explain: Thyroid hormones T4 and T3 contain 4 and 3 iodine atoms. Too little dietary iodine can cause hypothyroidism and an enlarged thyroid (goiter), which is why table salt is often iodized.

choices: Makes you sleepy and slows your heart
Lowers your blood sugar for storage
Raises heart rate and readies you for action
Slows your breathing to save oxygen

choices: In the front of the neck
At the base of the brain

questions.q: Which hormone drives bone and muscle growth in children?
questions.explain: Growth hormone from the pituitary promotes growth of bones and muscles, largely through IGF-1 made in the liver. Melatonin regulates sleep, glucagon raises blood sugar and ADH saves water.
questions.rick: Growth hormone. Named after what it does. A rare courtesy from scientists. Not from me, though.

questions.q: What causes type 1 diabetes?
choices: The pancreas makes too much insulin
The pancreas makes little or no insulin
The thyroid makes too little hormone
questions.explain: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas, so insulin is lacking and blood sugar rises. In type 2 the body still makes insulin but responds poorly to it.
questions.rick: Type 1: no insulin factory. Type 2: factory's fine, customers ignore the product. Got it?

questions.q: Click the pituitary gland.
questions.explain: The pituitary hangs below the brain, just beneath the hypothalamus, in a bony pocket of the skull. It controls many other glands.
questions.rick: Little pea under the brain. Clicked the whole brain? Close, but no *burp* Szechuan sauce for you.

questions.q: Click the thyroid gland.
questions.explain: The thyroid is the butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck, below the larynx (Adam's apple). It makes thyroid hormone, which sets metabolic rate.
questions.rick: Butterfly in the neck. Not the thymus, that's lower in the chest. T-words: still your nemesis.

questions.q: Click the organ that makes insulin.
questions.explain: The pancreas lies behind the stomach. Clusters of cells called islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon straight into the blood.
questions.rick: Pancreas, behind the stomach. Half digestion, half hormones. A multitasker. Try it sometime.

lessons.title: Hypothalamus and pituitary
lessons.fact: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary. The anterior pituitary makes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin. The posterior pituitary releases two hormones made by hypothalamic neurons: ADH (antidiuretic hormone, makes the kidneys save water) and oxytocin (uterine contractions in labor, milk let-down).
lessons.rick: Anterior makes its own stuff, posterior just stores the hypothalamus's stuff. Glorified *burp* storage unit.

lessons.title: Feedback loops
lessons.fact: Most hormones are controlled by negative feedback, like a thermostat. Example: hypothalamus TRH -> pituitary TSH -> thyroid T4 and T3. When T4/T3 rise, they inhibit TRH and TSH release, so output drops. Positive feedback is rarer: during labor, oxytocin drives contractions that trigger even more oxytocin.
lessons.rick: Negative feedback: the system shuts itself up when it's had enough. Try it sometime.

lessons.title: Steroid vs peptide hormones
lessons.fact: Peptide hormones (insulin, glucagon, ADH) are water-soluble and bind cell-surface receptors, many working via second messengers like cAMP. Steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone) are made from cholesterol, cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell to change gene transcription.
lessons.rick: Peptides ring the doorbell. Steroids walk right in and rewrite your DNA's to-do list. Rude, but effective.

lessons.title: Adrenals, kidneys and calcium
lessons.fact: Adrenal cortex: aldosterone (kidneys keep Na+, excrete K+) and cortisol (stress, raises glucose). Adrenal medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine. Kidneys release EPO, which boosts red blood cell production, and renin. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood Ca2+; calcitonin from the thyroid lowers it.
lessons.rick: PTH pulls calcium up, calcitonin tones it down. Like me and my liver: opposing forces.

questions.q: Which hormone is released from the POSTERIOR pituitary?
questions.explain: The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH, both made by neurons in the hypothalamus. TSH, growth hormone and prolactin are made by the anterior pituitary.
questions.rick: Posterior: oxytocin and ADH. That's it. Two. Like your functioning *burp* brain cells.

questions.q: Which hormone makes the kidneys reabsorb more water, producing concentrated urine?
questions.explain: ADH (vasopressin) makes the collecting ducts permeable to water, so more water returns to the blood and urine becomes concentrated. Alcohol suppresses ADH, which is why drinking makes you urinate more.
questions.rick: ADH: anti-diuretic, anti-peeing. Booze blocks it. I've done extensive personal research.

questions.q: High blood levels of T4 and T3 normally cause:
choices: Increased iodine uptake by the thyroid
questions.explain: Thyroid hormone feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering TRH and TSH. Less TSH means less stimulation of the thyroid, so output falls back toward normal.
questions.rick: High T4, low TSH. The thermostat turns the heater off. Basic household appliance logic.

questions.q: Steroid hormones such as cortisol and estrogen are made from:
questions.explain: All steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, progesterone, testosterone) are built from cholesterol. Peptide hormones are amino-acid chains, and thyroid hormone is made from iodinated tyrosine.
questions.rick: Cholesterol. That greasy stuff is the raw material for your whole hormonal personality.

questions.q: How do peptide hormones like glucagon usually act on target cells?
choices: Bind a surface receptor, often triggering a second messenger
Enter the nucleus and bind DNA directly
Dissolve through the membrane into the cytoplasm
Get broken down inside the cell to make ATP
questions.explain: Peptide hormones are water-soluble and can't cross the lipid membrane, so they bind cell-surface receptors; many then activate second messengers such as cAMP. Steroid and thyroid hormones act on intracellular receptors.
questions.rick: Peptides can't pass the greasy membrane, so they knock. The second messenger opens the door.

questions.q: Which hormone RAISES blood calcium?
questions.explain: PTH from the parathyroid glands raises blood Ca2+ by releasing it from bone, saving it in the kidney and activating vitamin D. Calcitonin from thyroid C cells has the opposite, weaker effect.
questions.rick: PTH raises calcium. Calcitonin TONES it down. The name is literally a hint. Read the names!

questions.q: Erythropoietin (EPO) from the kidneys stimulates:
questions.explain: When O2 delivery to the kidney drops (anemia, high altitude), kidney cells release EPO, which tells the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. Platelet production is driven mainly by thrombopoietin from the liver.
questions.rick: EPO: more red cells. Cyclists cheat with it. I just portal to a universe where I already won.

questions.q: Which is a classic example of POSITIVE feedback in the endocrine system?
choices: High T4 and T3 lowering TSH secretion
High blood glucose triggering insulin release
High blood Ca2+ suppressing PTH release
questions.explain: In labor, the baby pressing on the cervix triggers oxytocin release; oxytocin strengthens contractions, which press harder and release more oxytocin, until delivery ends the loop. The other three are negative feedback: the response switches off its own trigger.
questions.rick: Positive feedback: a loop that floors it until something gives. Usually a baby. Rarely a good *burp* idea otherwise.

questions.q: Click the glands that make cortisol and aldosterone.
questions.explain: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. Their outer cortex makes cortisol, aldosterone and androgens; the inner medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine.
questions.rick: On top of the kidneys. Two tiny hats full of stress juice. Very *burp* fashionable.

questions.q: Click the organ that makes most of the body's erythropoietin (EPO).
questions.explain: Specialized cells in the kidney cortex make most adult EPO (roughly 90%) when O2 delivery falls; the liver makes the rest. That's why chronic kidney disease often causes anemia.
questions.rick: Kidneys. Not just pee machines. Kidney failure, then anemia. Connect the dots, Morty-brain.

questions.q: Click the gland that makes calcitonin.
questions.explain: Calcitonin comes from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid. It lowers blood Ca2+ by inhibiting bone resorption, but in adult humans it plays only a minor role.
questions.rick: Thyroid again, different cells. C cells, C for calcitonin. Mnemonics this easy should be illegal.

lessons.title: Making thyroid hormone
lessons.fact: Thyroid follicular cells take up iodide via a Na+/I- symporter. Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes it, attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin and couples them into T4 (mostly) and T3. Tissues convert T4 to the more active T3 with deiodinases. T3 raises metabolic rate and heat production and sensitizes the heart to catecholamines.
lessons.rick: T4 is the prohormone, T3 does the real work. Like you and your *burp* lab partner.

lessons.title: The adrenal cortex zones
lessons.fact: Outside to inside: zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone (driven by angiotensin II and high K+); zona fasciculata makes cortisol (driven by ACTH); zona reticularis makes androgens such as DHEA. Mnemonic: salt, sugar, sex. The medulla's chromaffin cells make catecholamines, mostly epinephrine.
lessons.rick: Glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis: G-F-R, like the kidney. Salt, sugar, sex. Memorize or perish.

lessons.title: Insulin, glucagon, cortisol
lessons.fact: In beta cells, glucose is metabolized, ATP rises, ATP-sensitive K+ channels close, the cell depolarizes, Ca2+ enters and insulin is released. Insulin moves GLUT4 into muscle and fat cell membranes. Alpha cells make glucagon. Cortisol raises glucose (gluconeogenesis), breaks down muscle protein and suppresses immunity.
lessons.rick: Close the K+ channel, out comes insulin. Sulfonylurea drugs do exactly that. Pharmacology's just cheating.

lessons.title: Hormones from surprise organs
lessons.fact: Heart: stretched atria release ANP -> Na+ excretion, vasodilation. Kidney: renin, EPO, and calcitriol (active vitamin D, via 1-alpha-hydroxylase). Liver: IGF-1 in response to GH. Stomach: gastrin (G cells) and ghrelin (hunger). Small intestine: secretin, CCK, GIP. Fat tissue: leptin (satiety).
lessons.rick: Everything's a gland if you're desperate enough. The heart makes hormones. Even your fat has opinions.

questions.q: Which enzyme oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin?
questions.explain: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidizes iodide, iodinates tyrosine residues and couples them into T3 and T4. Deiodinases work in tissues, converting T4 to T3. Anti-TPO antibodies are typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.rick: TPO. Drugs like methimazole block it and the factory stalls. Pharmacology bonus, *burp* free of charge.

questions.q: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism because of antibodies that:
questions.explain: In Graves disease IgG antibodies mimic TSH and switch on the TSH receptor, driving hormone production and gland growth while real TSH is suppressed. Anti-TPO antibodies are typical of Hashimoto, which causes HYPOthyroidism.
questions.rick: Antibodies cosplaying as TSH. The thyroid can't tell. Neither could you, apparently.

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex makes aldosterone?
questions.explain: The zona glomerulosa, the outermost layer, makes aldosterone. Zona fasciculata makes cortisol, zona reticularis makes androgens, and the medulla makes catecholamines.
questions.rick: Outermost layer, salt hormone. Salt, sugar, sex, outside in. I gave you the mnemonic. Use it.

questions.q: What is the main stimulus for cortisol secretion?
questions.explain: ACTH from the anterior pituitary drives cortisol release from the zona fasciculata. Angiotensin II and high K+ are the main drivers of aldosterone, not cortisol.
questions.rick: ACTH: adrenocorticotropic hormone. Adrenal and cortex, right in the name. Read the label.

questions.q: In pancreatic beta cells, how does rising glucose trigger insulin release?
choices: More ATP opens K+(ATP) channels, hyperpolarizing the cell
Glucose binds a surface receptor that raises cAMP
Glucose directly fuses insulin vesicles with the membrane
More ATP closes K+(ATP) channels, depolarizing the cell
questions.explain: Glucose enters the beta cell and is metabolized; ATP rises and closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels. The cell depolarizes, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, and Ca2+ triggers insulin exocytosis. Sulfonylureas close the same channels.
questions.rick: Close K+ channels, depolarize, calcium, insulin. A domino chain even a Meeseeks could follow.

questions.q: Insulin increases glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and fat mainly by:
choices: Moving GLUT2 transporters into the cell membrane
Moving GLUT4 transporters into the cell membrane
questions.explain: Insulin signaling moves GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to the membrane of muscle and fat cells. GLUT2 (liver, gut, kidney) works without insulin, and SGLT1 absorbs glucose in the small intestine.
questions.rick: GLUT4, the insulin-sensitive one. Exercise moves it too, by the way. Not that you'd *burp* know.

questions.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released in response to:
choices: Low blood volume sensed by the kidneys
High blood glucose after a meal
Stretch of the atria from high blood volume
Low plasma Ca2+ sensed by the parathyroids
questions.explain: Volume overload stretches the atrial walls, and atrial muscle cells release ANP. It increases Na+ and water excretion, dilates vessels and opposes the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
questions.rick: Heart gets overstretched, tells the kidneys to dump salt. Smartest thing in your chest, honestly.

questions.q: Which is a typical effect of cortisol?
questions.explain: Cortisol raises blood glucose by boosting hepatic gluconeogenesis and breaking down muscle protein for amino acids. It suppresses the immune system (fewer circulating lymphocytes), which is why glucocorticoids are anti-inflammatory.
questions.rick: Cortisol: sugar up, muscle down, immune system nerfed. Chronic stress in a molecule. Basically me.

questions.q: Click the organ that releases atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP).
questions.explain: Atrial muscle cells in the heart release ANP when stretched by high blood volume. ANP promotes Na+ and water excretion by the kidneys and relaxes blood vessels.
questions.rick: The heart. A pump with a side hustle in endocrinology. Show-off.

questions.q: Click the organ that makes most of the body's ghrelin, the hunger hormone.
questions.explain: Ghrelin is made mainly by cells in the stomach (mostly the fundus). Levels rise before meals and stimulate appetite and growth hormone release. The stomach's G cells also secrete gastrin.
questions.rick: Ghrelin: your stomach growling at your brain. Mine's mostly growling for *burp* Szechuan sauce.

questions.q: Click the organ that makes most circulating IGF-1 in response to growth hormone.
questions.explain: Growth hormone acts on the liver to make insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which carries out much of GH's growth effect on bone and cartilage. The liver is the main source of circulating IGF-1.
questions.rick: Liver. GH sends the order, the liver does the actual work. Typical management structure.

lessons.title: Cushing syndrome
lessons.fact: Cortisol excess: central obesity, moon face, purple striae, high glucose, hypertension. Most common cause: glucocorticoid drugs (low ACTH). Endogenous: pituitary ACTH adenoma (Cushing disease), ectopic ACTH (e.g. small cell lung cancer), adrenal tumor (low ACTH). High-dose dexamethasone suppresses pituitary but not ectopic ACTH.
lessons.rick: Dexamethasone test: pituitary adenomas still obey feedback, ectopic tumors don't. Rebels without a *burp* receptor.

lessons.title: Adrenal failure and Conn
lessons.fact: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison): low cortisol and aldosterone -> hypotension, low Na+, high K+; high ACTH darkens the skin. Secondary (pituitary, e.g. Sheehan postpartum infarction): low ACTH, no darkening, aldosterone near normal. Conn (primary hyperaldosteronism): hypertension, low K+, low renin.
lessons.rick: Dark skin plus high K+? Adrenals dead, ACTH screaming. Pituitary problem? Paler, quieter. Labs tell stories.

lessons.title: Water: DI vs SIADH
lessons.fact: ADH binds V2 receptors in the collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2. Diabetes insipidus = lots of dilute urine: central (no ADH; urine concentrates after desmopressin) or nephrogenic (kidney resistant, e.g. lithium; no response). SIADH (e.g. small cell lung cancer): too much ADH, concentrated urine, euvolemic hyponatremia.
lessons.rick: DI: pee like a firehose. SIADH: hoard water till sodium drowns. Opposite disasters, same *burp* hormone.

lessons.title: Calcium and insulin pearls
lessons.fact: PTH raises Ca2+ (bone resorption, distal tubule Ca2+ reabsorption, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase -> calcitriol) and lowers phosphate. Insulin drives K+ into cells, so DKA shows normal-high serum K+ despite total-body K+ loss. Proinsulin splits into insulin + C-peptide: C-peptide is high in insulinoma, low after injected insulin.
lessons.rick: Calcium, potassium, C-peptide: three exam traps, one lesson. I'm basically doing your homework.

questions.q: Weight gain, purple striae, high cortisol and high ACTH. High-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol. Most likely cause?
choices: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer
questions.explain: High ACTH means ACTH-dependent disease; suppression by high-dose dexamethasone means the source still obeys feedback: a pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease). Ectopic ACTH does not suppress; adrenal tumors and prednisone give LOW ACTH.
questions.rick: High ACTH that still suppresses: pituitary. The adenoma's a little obedient. Ectopic tumors obey nobody.

questions.q: Fatigue, low blood pressure and darkening skin; Na+ 128 mEq/L, K+ 6.0 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Low aldosterone gives low Na+, high K+ and hypotension; high ACTH (POMC, which also yields MSH) darkens skin. Secondary insufficiency has low ACTH: no darkening and usually normal K+. SIADH does not raise K+.
questions.rick: Tan without a beach plus high K+? The adrenals are toast. Addison. *burp* Next.

questions.q: Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, high aldosterone and LOW plasma renin. Most likely cause?
questions.explain: Autonomous aldosterone (adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia) retains Na+, wastes K+ and H+, and suppresses renin. Renal artery stenosis has HIGH renin; licorice lets cortisol act on aldosterone receptors, so aldosterone is LOW; Addison causes hypotension.
questions.rick: High aldo, low renin: the adrenal's freelancing. Conn. If renin is high, check the kidney's plumbing instead.

questions.q: After head trauma: polyuria; urine stays dilute (100 mOsm/kg) despite water restriction but rises to 450 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. Diagnosis?
questions.explain: In central DI the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary fails to release ADH, so urine stays dilute with water restriction, but the kidney responds to desmopressin (synthetic ADH). Nephrogenic DI does not respond; primary polydipsia concentrates with restriction.
questions.rick: Responds to desmopressin, so the kidneys work. The ADH supply chain's broken. Central. Easy.

questions.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer has Na+ 122 mEq/L, normal volume status and inappropriately concentrated urine. Diagnosis?
questions.explain: Small cell lung cancer can secrete ADH ectopically. Excess ADH makes the kidneys retain free water: euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine. DI gives dilute urine and high-normal Na+; primary polydipsia gives maximally dilute urine.
questions.rick: Tumor pumping ADH, kidneys hoarding water, sodium diluted. SIADH. Small cell: paraneoplastic overachiever.

questions.q: A patient with end-stage chronic kidney disease most likely has which pattern of serum values?
choices: High Ca2+, low phosphate, high PTH
High Ca2+, high phosphate, low PTH
Low Ca2+, high phosphate, high PTH
Low Ca2+, high phosphate, low PTH
questions.explain: Failing kidneys retain phosphate and make little calcitriol (less 1-alpha-hydroxylase), so Ca2+ falls and the parathyroids overwork: secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal osteodystrophy). High Ca2+ + low phosphate + high PTH is primary; low Ca2+ + low PTH is hypoparathyroidism.
questions.rick: Dead kidneys hoard phosphate and skip the vitamin D. The parathyroids panic. Secondary hyperparathyroidism, *burp* genius.

questions.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, why is serum K+ often normal or high even though total-body K+ is depleted?
choices: Insulin lack and hyperosmolality shift K+ out of cells
The kidneys stop excreting K+ during ketoacidosis
High insulin levels push K+ out of cells
Ketones block K+ excretion in the urine
questions.explain: Insulin normally drives K+ into cells via the Na+/K+-ATPase; without it, and with hyperosmolality pulling water and K+ out, K+ leaves cells. Meanwhile osmotic diuresis wastes K+ in urine, so total-body K+ is low and falls fast once insulin is given.
questions.rick: Insulin is the K+ bouncer: shoves it into cells. Fire the bouncer, K+ floods the plasma. Rehire him, it crashes.

questions.q: A hypoglycemic nurse has high serum insulin but LOW C-peptide. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Beta cells release insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts, so insulinoma and sulfonylureas raise both. Pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide, and the high insulin suppresses the patient's own secretion, so C-peptide is low.
questions.rick: No C-peptide, no pancreas involved. Somebody's been *burp* injecting. Medicine's a detective show, genius.

questions.q: Click the gland that infarcts in Sheehan syndrome after severe postpartum hemorrhage.
questions.explain: The pituitary enlarges in pregnancy and is vulnerable to low blood flow. Massive blood loss at delivery can infarct it: often the first sign is failure to lactate (no prolactin), then hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency.
questions.rick: Pituitary. Pregnancy makes it big and hungry for blood. Cut the supply and the whole empire falls.

questions.q: Click the organ where 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes active vitamin D (calcitriol).
questions.explain: The liver makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D; the kidney's proximal tubule adds the second hydroxyl via 1-alpha-hydroxylase (stimulated by PTH). That's why chronic kidney disease causes low calcitriol and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.rick: Kidneys finish vitamin D. Liver starts it, kidney closes. Kidneys fail, calcium chaos. Elementary.

questions.q: Click the organ whose S cells release secretin when stomach acid arrives.
questions.explain: S cells in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, release secretin in response to acid. Secretin makes the pancreas secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize it.
questions.rick: Duodenum, small intestine. Acid arrives, secretin calls the pancreas for baking soda. Chemistry, Morty-brain.

parts.name: Dendrites
parts.desc: Branched extensions of the neuron that receive incoming signals, mostly at synapses on their surface, and carry them toward the cell body.
parts.rick: Dendrites: the listening branches. More receptive than you'll ever be.

parts.name: Soma (Cell Body)
parts.desc: The neuron's cell body. Contains the nucleus and most organelles, including clumps of rough ER (Nissl substance), and integrates the incoming signals.
parts.rick: The cell body. Where the neuron keeps its nucleus and its *burp* priorities.

parts.name: Nucleus
parts.desc: Holds the neuron's DNA. Mature neurons generally do not divide. Typically large and pale with a prominent nucleolus, reflecting heavy protein synthesis.
parts.rick: DNA headquarters. Neurons mostly never divide again. Commitment issues? Not them.

parts.name: Axon Hillock
parts.desc: Cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the soma. The initial segment just beyond it is packed with voltage-gated Na+ channels, so action potentials usually start in this zone.
parts.rick: Trigger zone. All the inputs get summed here, then it decides: fire or not. Binary. Respect.

parts.name: Axon
parts.desc: The single long process that conducts action potentials away from the cell body to the axon terminals. Some axons are about 1 m long, from the spinal cord to the foot.
parts.rick: The long cable. Some run from your spine to your toes. Longer than your attention span, easily.

parts.name: Myelin Sheath
parts.desc: Fatty insulating wrap made by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS). It raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so impulses jump node to node much faster.
parts.rick: Fatty insulation. Makes signals fast. Fat being useful for once, Morty-brain.

parts.name: Node of Ranvier
parts.desc: Short gaps between myelin segments, packed with voltage-gated Na+ channels. The action potential regenerates here and jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction).
parts.rick: Gaps where the spike recharges and hops. Portal tech, biological edition.

parts.name: Axon Terminal
parts.desc: Swollen end of an axon branch filled with neurotransmitter vesicles. Ca2+ entering through voltage-gated channels triggers vesicle fusion and transmitter release.
parts.rick: Where the electrical signal turns chemical. Calcium pulls the *burp* trigger.

parts.name: Synapse
parts.desc: Junction where a neuron passes its signal to another cell: presynaptic terminal, a narrow synaptic cleft (roughly 20-40 nm), and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors.
parts.rick: The gap where neurons talk without touching. Like you and social skills.

parts.name: Frontal Lobe
parts.desc: Front of each hemisphere, ahead of the central sulcus. Planning, judgment, personality and voluntary movement (motor cortex); on the dominant side, speech production (Broca area).
parts.rick: Planning, judgment, personality. Yours is apparently on *burp* airplane mode.

parts.name: Parietal Lobe
parts.desc: Between the central sulcus and the occipital lobe. Processes touch, pain, temperature and body position (somatosensory cortex) and spatial awareness.
parts.rick: Touch and spatial sense. It knows where your hand is. Wish it knew where your brain was.

parts.name: Temporal Lobe
parts.desc: Below the lateral sulcus. Hearing (primary auditory cortex), language comprehension (Wernicke area on the dominant side) and memory (hippocampus on its inner side).
parts.rick: Hearing and memory. Remember this, would you? It's literally the memory lobe.

parts.name: Occipital Lobe
parts.desc: Back of the cerebrum. Contains the primary visual cortex, which receives input from the eyes relayed through the thalamus.

parts.name: Cerebellum
parts.desc: Below the occipital lobes, behind the brainstem. Coordinates movement, balance and posture and helps motor learning; damage causes clumsy movement (ataxia) on the same side.

parts.name: Pons
parts.desc: Middle part of the brainstem, between midbrain and medulla. Relays signals from cerebrum to cerebellum, helps regulate breathing, and holds nuclei of cranial nerves V, VI, VII (and part of VIII).

parts.name: Medulla Oblongata
parts.desc: Lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord. Holds cardiovascular and respiratory centers, and the pyramids; most corticospinal fibers cross at their lower end.

parts.name: Spinal Cord
parts.desc: Continues from the medulla down the vertebral canal to about L1-L2 in adults. Carries ascending sensory and descending motor tracts, runs reflexes, and gives off 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

parts.name: Central Sulcus
parts.desc: Deep groove separating the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe, and the precentral (motor) gyrus from the postcentral (sensory) gyrus.

parts.name: Lateral Sulcus
parts.desc: Also called the Sylvian fissure. Deep groove separating the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above; the insula lies hidden deep inside it.

parts.name: Precentral Gyrus
parts.desc: Ridge just in front of the central sulcus: the primary motor cortex. Its upper motor neurons send axons down the corticospinal tract to move the opposite side of the body.

parts.name: Postcentral Gyrus
parts.desc: Ridge just behind the central sulcus: the primary somatosensory cortex. Receives touch, pain, temperature and position from the opposite side, mapped as the sensory homunculus.

parts.name: Broca Area
parts.desc: Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. Speech production; damage causes non-fluent (expressive) aphasia with fairly intact comprehension.

parts.name: Wernicke Area
parts.desc: Posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. Language comprehension; damage causes fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension.

parts.name: Brain
parts.desc: Control center of the nervous system. Its hypothalamus is also an endocrine organ: it makes releasing and inhibiting hormones for the pituitary plus ADH and oxytocin. The pineal gland makes melatonin.

parts.name: Pituitary Gland

parts.name: Thyroid Gland
parts.desc: Butterfly-shaped gland in front of the trachea, below the larynx. Follicular cells make T4 and T3 (metabolic rate); parafollicular C cells make calcitonin.

parts.name: Thymus
parts.desc: Gland in the upper chest behind the sternum, where T cells mature and learn self-tolerance. Large in children, mostly replaced by fat in adults; makes thymic hormones (thymosins).

parts.name: Heart
parts.desc: Muscular pump in the middle of the chest. Also endocrine: stretched atria release atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), which promotes Na+ and water excretion.

parts.name: Lungs
parts.desc: Paired gas-exchange organs in the chest. Their capillary endothelium is rich in angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), a major site where angiotensin I becomes angiotensin II.
parts.rick: Air bags with an ACE up their sleeve. Literally. Angiotensin I in, angiotensin II out.

parts.name: Liver
parts.desc: Largest internal organ, upper right abdomen. Stores glycogen, makes bile and plasma proteins. Hormone-wise it makes IGF-1 (in response to GH), angiotensinogen and hepcidin.
parts.rick: The body's chemical plant. Mine's been working *burp* overtime since roughly forever.

parts.name: Stomach
parts.desc: J-shaped organ in the upper left abdomen. Secretes acid and pepsinogen; G cells make gastrin (boosts acid), and the stomach is the main source of ghrelin, the hunger hormone.
parts.rick: Acid pit that growls for food via ghrelin. Mine growls for Szechuan sauce.

parts.name: Spleen
parts.desc: Upper left abdomen, behind the stomach. Largest lymphoid organ: filters blood, removes old red blood cells and fights blood-borne bacteria, especially encapsulated ones.
parts.rick: Blood filter and red-cell graveyard. Lose it and encapsulated bacteria throw a party.

parts.name: Pancreas
parts.desc: Behind the stomach. The exocrine part makes digestive enzymes; the islets of Langerhans make insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha cells) and somatostatin (delta cells).
parts.rick: Enzymes out one door, insulin out the other. Two jobs, zero complaints. Learn from it.

parts.name: Adrenal Glands
parts.desc: One on top of each kidney. Cortex: aldosterone, cortisol and androgens. Medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine.
parts.rick: Tiny hats on the kidneys pumping stress hormones. Mine are *burp* permanently maxed.

parts.name: Kidneys
parts.desc: Paired organs at the back of the upper abdomen. They filter blood into urine and release renin, erythropoietin (EPO) and active vitamin D (calcitriol).
parts.rick: Filters that moonlight as hormone factories: renin, EPO, vitamin D. Overachievers.

parts.name: Small Intestine
parts.desc: Several meters of tube (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) where most digestion and absorption happen. Its cells release gut hormones such as secretin, CCK and GIP.
parts.rick: Where food actually gets absorbed. Meters of gut doing your nutritional *burp* homework.

parts.name: Large Intestine
parts.desc: Cecum, colon and rectum. Absorbs water and electrolytes, houses gut bacteria (some make vitamin K), and forms and stores feces.
parts.rick: Water reclaimer and bacteria hotel. Also the end of the line. Like this conversation, soon.

parts.name: Urinary Bladder
parts.desc: Hollow muscular sac in the pelvis that stores urine from the ureters. Its detrusor muscle contracts (parasympathetic) to empty it through the urethra.
parts.rick: A stretchy bag for pee. Not complicated. Even you got this one, right?

parts.name: Lymph Nodes
parts.desc: Bean-shaped filters along lymphatic vessels, clustered in the neck, armpits, groin and abdomen. B and T cells meet antigens here; nodes swell during infections.
parts.rick: Immune checkpoints. Swollen nodes mean the immune system's busy. Busier than you, anyway.
